body:
Rule. Command wraps an action and its arguments as an object with an execute method, and often undo. Callers create commands and hand them to an invoker that runs, queues, or logs them. Use it when you need history, macros, or deferred execution of operations.

Why it matters. Bare method calls cannot be stored, undone, or replayed easily. Commands make actions first-class. Without undo or queue needs, a plain function is simpler.

Worked example. Editor holds a stack. TypeCommand("a") on buffer length 0 execute inserts a at the cursor and undo deletes it. BoldCommand execute toggles bold on the selection; undo toggles back. Macro runs a list of commands in order and undoes in reverse. Remote: serialize TransferCommand(from, to, amount) onto a queue; a worker execute applies it idempotently with a command id. GUI buttons bind to command instances rather than hard-coding editor methods, so the same PasteCommand can sit on a menu and a shortcut.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. Keep the tone focused and honest.  Walk one concrete path with numbers before generalizing. When to use. Use command for editors with undo, job queues of domain actions, and GUI action binding. Use it when you must log or audit the intent separately from execution.

When to refuse. Refuse command objects for every trivial one-line call. Refuse execute methods that are not reversible when the product promise is undo. Refuse commands that mutate shared state without capturing enough for undo. Refuse command when an observer or a direct call expresses the need better.
